opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something we've been thinking about a lot. The common intuition is that more training is always better: you pretrain longer, you fine-tune more, you do more RL, and the model just gets stronger. When you look closely, though, there's a tension between getting better at producing the single best answer and keeping the ability to explore a range of different answers.

Take fine-tuning on reasoning tasks. If you only measure whether the model's top answer is right, the pass@1 accuracy, you see steady improvement with more training. If you instead sample many times and ask whether *any* of those attempts is correct, the pass@k for larger k, you often see that metric plateau or even go down as training continues. The model is becoming more confident and more peaked. It collapses onto a few modes, so all its samples start looking alike. If those modes are wrong for a given problem, sampling more won't save you.

The way I think about it is that training with cross-entropy, or with reward maximization in RL, pushes probability mass toward whatever the model currently thinks is best. That sharpening helps on average, but it costs you the tail of the distribution, and the tail is where the alternative strategies live. Those alternatives are exactly what you'd want if you plan to use test-time compute, sampling, search, or verification, to find a correct solution.

This connects to some of our work on overtraining more broadly. We've seen that past a certain point, pretraining on more tokens can make models harder to adapt downstream. The parameters become more sensitive, and fine-tuning then causes more forgetting or degradation. So "more training" isn't monotonic in every property you care about. You're trading off different capabilities.

The practical takeaway is that we should be careful about how we evaluate. If your deployment involves sampling many candidates and picking one, you shouldn't optimize and select checkpoints purely on greedy accuracy. You want to preserve diversity on purpose. There are a few ways to do that, like stopping earlier, regularizing toward the base model, ensembling or interpolating checkpoints, or designing objectives that directly reward coverage rather than only the top answer. Treating diversity as something to protect, rather than a side effect, makes a real difference in how much you get out of test-time scaling.

r001.rationale: It says pass@k can plateau or decline as training continues, so sampling more attempts may not find a correct answer.

r002.rationale: It says training collapses samples onto a few modes so attempts look alike, and when those modes are wrong, sampling more will not help.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So this is something we've been thinking about a lot, and the short version is that additional training — whether it's more pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, or RL — tends to make models sharper but also narrower. We've been calling one version of this "catastrophic overtraining," but the more general phenomenon is that as you optimize a model harder on a particular distribution, you're collapsing its output distribution toward whatever that training signal rewards.

Let me try to unpack why that happens. Think about what the objective is actually asking for. If you're doing SFT on a set of worked solutions, you're asking the model to put as much probability mass as possible on those specific solutions. If you're doing RL with a verifier, you're asking it to put mass on things that get the reward. Neither objective says anything about preserving the spread of the distribution. So the natural thing that happens is the model finds a mode that works and concentrates there. You'll see this very clearly if you look at pass@1 versus pass@k. Pass@1 goes up — the model gets better at producing its single best guess. But pass@k, for large k, often goes flat or even goes down relative to the base model, because the samples you're drawing are now highly correlated with each other. You're not really getting k different attempts; you're getting roughly the same attempt k times with minor variations.

And that matters because a lot of the ways we want to use these models — search, best-of-n, self-consistency, agentic exploration — depend on the model actually being able to propose genuinely different things. If the diversity is gone, more inference compute doesn't buy you much. So there's this tension where the training that makes the model look better on a leaderboard can make it a worse engine for test-time scaling.

The way I try to understand it mechanistically is through the lens of what the base model already encodes. The base model, after pretraining, has this very broad distribution — it's seen many ways of solving a problem, many styles, many partial approaches. Post-training is mostly reshaping that distribution rather than adding fundamentally new knowledge. And reshaping can be done in a way that's more or less destructive. Larger learning rates, longer training, lower-entropy targets all push toward collapse. We've found that even the amount of pretraining matters here — a model that's been pretrained longer can actually be more sensitive to fine-tuning, in the sense that the same fine-tuning perturbation causes a larger drop in its original capabilities. So "more training is always better" is just not true once you account for what happens downstream.

A few things we've looked at to measure this more carefully. One is to not just look at accuracy but to look at the entropy of the output distribution, or at the number of distinct correct solutions you get across samples. Another is to look at calibration — does the model's confidence track whether it's right? Collapsed models tend to be overconfident, which is another symptom of the same thing. And then there's the question of whether you're losing diversity in a way that's recoverable. Sometimes it's just a temperature issue and you can sample it back. But often it's not — the alternative modes have been really pushed down, and no amount of sampling brings them back.

On the intervention side, I think there are a few promising directions. One is to explicitly regularize toward the base model, or toward some reference distribution, so you're constrained in how far you can collapse. KL penalties in RLHF are a crude version of this. Another is to change what you're rewarding — instead of rewarding the single best answer, reward sets of answers for being both correct and different from each other. And a third is to think more carefully about which data you're training on. A lot of the diversity loss comes from fine-tuning on data that's itself very homogeneous — you know, thousands of solutions written in exactly the same style by the same model. If your SFT data is a monoculture, the model becomes a monoculture.

So I guess the way I'd summarize it is: additional training is a trade. You're trading breadth for depth on the training distribution. Sometimes that's exactly what you want. But if what you care about is the model's ability to explore, to try things it hasn't been told to try, then you have to be very deliberate about that, because the default behavior of our training pipelines is to erode it.

r001.rationale: It says pass@k can go flat or decline relative to the base model as samples become highly correlated, so additional training can worsen results across multiple queries.

r002.rationale: It says samples may repeat roughly the same attempt, but does not state that the repeated solution is incorrect.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by additional training. Getting better at producing one good answer isn’t necessarily the same as getting better at exploring different solutions. You could have a model that, after more training, is more likely to get the answer right on its first attempt, but when you sample it multiple times, those attempts all look very similar.

So there are two things I’d want to measure: how good is a single attempt, and how much do you gain by allowing the model to try again? If training reinforces a particular way of solving a problem, it could improve the first while reducing the benefit of additional attempts. Ideally, we’d want training that improves the quality of the solutions without losing alternative approaches that might be useful on a harder problem.

r001.rationale: The response says training could reduce the benefit of additional attempts, but does not clearly state that performance across multiple queries worsens.

r002.rationale: It says repeated samples may look similar, but does not say they repeat the same incorrect solution or tie that outcome to excessive training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between getting better at producing one good answer and getting better at exploring different ways to solve a problem. Additional training can improve the first without necessarily improving the second.

For example, if you sample several responses, you might find that the trained model succeeds more often on each individual attempt, but those attempts are more similar to one another. So you get less benefit from trying again. A model with lower single-attempt accuracy might actually solve more problems across many attempts because it explores a broader set of solutions.

That means we should look at both: how good is the first answer, and how much additional coverage do we get as we allow more attempts? Otherwise, an improvement in the usual accuracy metric can hide a loss in the model’s ability to try diverse approaches.

r001.rationale: It says additional training can make attempts more similar and reduce the benefit of trying again, allowing a less accurate but broader model to solve more problems across multiple attempts.

r002.rationale: It describes attempts becoming more similar, but does not say they repeat the same incorrect solution.
